# The Handover From Sales to Delivery

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-handover-from-sales-to-delivery/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-15 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Forrester found that 81% of B2B buyers are dissatisfied with the provider they chose, and win-loss interviews suggest some won customers are already at risk on signature. Much of that risk is created at the handover, when the deal team's knowledge of promises, stakeholders and concessions fails to reach delivery. This piece sets out a handover pack, a timing rule and a measure that tells you whether it is working.

The handover from sales to delivery is the point where a won deal becomes work, and where most of what the deal team learned is lost. A good handover passes on more than the contract: the promises made, the buying group and its politics, the concessions and why they were granted, the risks raised, and what success means to the buyer. Forrester's 2024 research found 81% of B2B buyers dissatisfied with the provider they chose. The handover cannot fix a bad sale, but it is the cheapest place to stop a good sale turning into a disappointed customer.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

In most firms of 20 to 500 people, the person who wins the work is not the person who does it. That is true in software, where an account executive hands to an onboarding team, and in services, where a partner who sold the engagement passes it to a project lead. Even where the seller stays involved, a new group of people starts making decisions about the client.

The handover is the moment knowledge has to cross that line. In [*Handovers are where reasoning pours out*](https://lowob.com/research/handovers-are-where-reasoning-pours-out/) we argued that the facts usually survive a handover while the reasons behind them do not. The commercial version of that problem is sharp, because the reasons often carry money: a discount granted against a promise, a timeline agreed to beat a rival, a scope line dropped to get under a budget.

## What goes wrong, and how often

The evidence on what buyers experience after signing is thin but consistent.

Forrester's *State of Business Buying, 2024* found that 81% of buyers were dissatisfied with the provider they chose at the end of the purchase process, and that 86% of purchases stalled at some point. It put the average buying group at 13 people, with 89% of purchases involving two or more departments. Delivery teams inherit all of those people, most of whom they have never met. Forrester's analyst Barbara Winters, writing on the same research, added that the dissatisfaction ran to 91% among Gen Z and Millennial buyers, and that buyers were not satisfied with the technology, domain and industry expertise providers demonstrated. Expertise is exactly what a delivery team shows first, and it shows less of it when it starts without the deal team's context.

A Showpad interview with Clozd's co-founder, published in August 2026, reported that about 10% of closed-won customers were already at risk when interviewed after the decision, often because of implementation problems or doubts about the solution. It is a vendor figure without a published sample, so we treat it as indicative. It describes a customer who signed while unconvinced, and a delivery team that may not know.

Gartner's 2026 survey of 646 B2B buyers found that buyers with high decision confidence were twice as likely to report a high-quality deal. Decision confidence is built during the sale and either reinforced or eroded in the first weeks of delivery. The handover decides which.

| Failure at handover | What delivery experiences | Typical cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Promise not passed on | Client cites a commitment nobody in delivery recognises | Unplanned scope, or a credibility loss in week one |
| Concession without its reason | Delivery treats a discounted line as standard | Margin given away twice |
| Stakeholder map missing | The sceptic in the buying group is not engaged | Late objections, slower sign-off |
| Success criteria vague | Delivery measures outputs; client expected outcomes | Dispute at the first review |
| Known risk not flagged | Risk surfaces as a surprise | Rework, escalation, early churn |

## The cost shows up in delivery and renewal

For services firms the cost of a weak handover appears first in utilisation. SPI Research's 2026 benchmark, published with Deltek, put average billable utilisation at 66.4%, the lowest in nearly two decades, against 75% for high performers. SPI's report page adds that top firms achieved 82% on-time delivery in the prior year, which sets a delivery standard a handover either supports or undermines. Not all of the utilisation gap is handovers. But hours spent rediscovering what the client was promised are hours nobody can bill, and they cluster at the start of an engagement.

For recurring-revenue firms the cost appears at renewal. SaaS Capital's 2025 benchmarks put median net revenue retention at 102% for companies with annual contract values of $25,000 to $50,000. A customer whose first ninety days were a series of surprises is less likely to be one who expands. Part 24 of this series covered renewals and expansion; the handover is where the renewal conversation starts.

The Bridge Group's 2026 study adds a structural point. It found 38% of account executives now own renewal and expansion, nearly double the 2024 share. Where the seller will come back to the account, a poor handover is a cost the seller pays later.

> The facts survive the handover. The reasons do not, and in commercial work the reasons carry the money.

## What a handover pack should hold

A handover pack is short. Its value comes from containing the things that are in nobody's system yet. Most of them are reasons.

| Section | What it records | Who writes it | Why delivery needs it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| What we sold | Scope, exclusions, and the reason for each exclusion | Deal lead | Prevents excluded work drifting back in |
| What we promised | Every commitment made in meetings or emails, verbatim where possible | Deal lead | These are the client's expectations, whatever the contract says |
| What success means | The buyer's own measure, in their words | Deal lead, confirmed with the buyer | Lets delivery report against the right outcome |
| The buying group | Who decided, who influenced, who was sceptical and why | Deal lead | Delivery needs to win the sceptic, not only the sponsor |
| Concessions | Every discount or term beyond standard, with the reason and the approver | Deal desk or revenue lead | Stops delivery treating a concession as a precedent |
| Risks | Known doubts, competing priorities, dependencies on the client | Deal lead and delivery lead together | Turns surprises into managed risks |
| Open questions | What nobody knows yet | Both | Gives the kickoff an agenda |

Two of these sections connect to other parts of the commercial system. Concessions come from discount governance: if each exception was recorded with its reason and approver, the handover can link to that record rather than reconstruct it. Promises and success criteria come from the proposal, which is one reason Part 22 treated proposal standards as part of the commercial system: a proposal that states outcomes in the buyer's own words gives the handover something to copy rather than reconstruct.

[*The context layer, followed through one account*](https://lowob.com/research/the-context-layer-followed-through-one-account/) showed how an account's history ends up scattered across inboxes, recordings, proposal versions and memory. The handover pack is the commercial team's deliberate answer: one document, written once, that delivery can trust.

## Timing: before signature, not after

Most handovers happen after the contract is signed. By then the deal team's attention has moved to the next opportunity, and the incentive to write anything down has passed.

Three timing rules work better.

**Introduce delivery before the final proposal.** On deals above a set value, a delivery lead should meet the buyer before the proposal is final. That tests whether what is being sold can be delivered, and it lets the buyer meet the person they will work with. It also addresses the implementation doubts that win-loss interviews find late in the cycle.

**Write the pack before signature.** Make a draft handover pack a condition of moving a deal to its final stage. The seller still has the context and still has a reason to cooperate.

**Hold a joint kickoff.** The first client meeting after signature should include the deal lead, the delivery lead and the buyer's sponsor. The deal lead's job in that meeting is to restate the promises and the success measure in front of everyone.

| Deal size | Delivery involvement before signature | Pack | Kickoff |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Small, standard scope | None | Template, completed by the seller | Delivery-led |
| Mid-size or custom scope | Review of the draft proposal | Full pack, reviewed by delivery | Joint |
| Large or strategic | Meeting with the buyer before the final proposal | Full pack, signed off by both leads | Joint, with the buyer's sponsor |

## Measuring whether the handover works

A completed form is not a measure. The measure is what delivery finds that the pack did not tell it.

Ask the delivery lead to log every material surprise in the first 30 days: a promise not in the pack, a stakeholder not mapped, a risk not flagged, a concession not explained. Count them per engagement and review the count monthly with the revenue lead. A falling count means the pack is working. A count that stays high in one segment or for one seller is a coaching conversation.

Keep the definition of a material surprise narrow: something that changed scope, cost, timeline or a key relationship, and that someone on the deal team knew before signature. Minor gaps in detail do not count. A narrow definition keeps the log honest and stops it turning into a complaints list about sales.

Two lagging measures confirm the trend: time to first value, defined as the buyer defines it in the pack, and early churn or early escalation. Both arrive later and are noisier, which is why the surprise count is the one to watch weekly.

The surprise log is also a decision record. Each recurring surprise is a reason to change the pack, the proposal standard or the qualification questions, and the change should be recorded with an owner and a check date, as in [*The commercial decisions worth recording*](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/).

Illustrative example: the concession that crossed the line

Decision
:   Add a concessions section to the handover pack, linked to the discount approval record, and make it a condition of the final deal stage.

Reason and owner
:   Delivery logged the same surprise on three engagements in a quarter: a reduced day rate agreed in exchange for a case study, which delivery did not know to request. Owned by the revenue lead, agreed with the head of delivery.

What changed
:   Concessions now arrive with their reason and their condition. Surprises per engagement are reviewed monthly.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size consulting firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Pass on reasons, not only facts.** Why a discount, exclusion or timeline was agreed matters more than the fact that it was.
- **Write the pack before signature.** After signature, the context and the incentive both leave.
- **Introduce delivery early on large deals.** It tests deliverability and builds the buyer's confidence.
- **Count surprises.** Material surprises in the first 30 days are the honest measure of a handover.

Gateway card

### Before the next deal crosses to delivery

- A one-page handover pack template with the seven sections above
- A draft pack required before the final deal stage
- Concessions linked to their approval record, with the reason
- The buyer's success measure written in their words
- A joint kickoff for mid-size and larger deals
- A 30-day surprise log reviewed monthly by revenue and delivery leads
